verses.text: But after a while, in the time of wheat harvest, Samson visited his wife with a young goat. He said, “I will go in to my wife’s room.” But her father wouldn’t allow him to go in.
Her father said, “I most certainly thought that you utterly hated her; therefore I gave her to your companion. Isn’t her younger sister more beautiful than she? Please take her, instead.”
Samson said to them, “This time I will be blameless in the case of the Philistines, when I harm them.”
Samson went and caught three hundred foxes, and took torches, and turned tail to tail, and put a torch in the middle between every two tails.
When he had set the torches on fire, he let them go into the standing grain of the Philistines, and burned up both the shocks and the standing grain, and also the olive groves.

Then the Philistines said, “Who has done this?” They said, “Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because he has taken his wife, and given her to his companion.” The Philistines came up, and burned her and her father with fire.
Samson said to them, “If you behave like this, surely I will take revenge on you, and after that I will cease.”
He struck them hip and thigh with a great slaughter; and he went down and lived in the cave in Etam’s rock.
Then the Philistines went up, encamped in Judah, and spread themselves in Lehi.
The men of Judah said, “Why have you come up against us?” They said, “We have come up to bind Samson, to do to him as he has done to us.”

Then three thousand men of Judah went down to the cave in Etam’s rock, and said to Samson, “Don’t you know that the Philistines are rulers over us? What then is this that you have done to us?” He said to them, “As they did to me, so I have done to them.”
They said to him, “We have come down to bind you, that we may deliver you into the hand of the Philistines.” Samson said to them, “Swear to me that you will not attack me yourselves.”
They spoke to him, saying, “No; but we will bind you securely, and deliver you into their hands; but surely we will not kill you.” They bound him with two new ropes, and brought him up from the rock.

When he came to Lehi, the Philistines shouted as they met him. Then Yahweh’s Spirit came mightily on him, and the ropes that were on his arms became as flax that was burned with fire, and his bands dropped from off his hands.
He found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, put out his hand, took it, and struck a thousand men with it.
Samson said, “With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps on heaps; with the jawbone of a donkey I have struck a thousand men.”
When he had finished speaking, he threw the jawbone out of his hand; and that place was called Ramath Lehi.
He was very thirsty, and called on Yahweh, and said, “You have given this great deliverance by the hand of your servant; and now shall I die of thirst, and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?”

But God split the hollow place that is in Lehi, and water came out of it. When he had drunk, his spirit came again, and he revived. Therefore its name was called En Hakkore, which is in Lehi, to this day.
He judged Israel twenty years in the days of the Philistines.

footnotes.content: Samson brings a young goat to his wife—a small gesture of tenderness, yet the door is shut to him. How often we move toward reconciliation only to find ourselves turned away. But look: his love doesn't harden into bitterness immediately. There's a moment here where something better could happen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Her father speaks with the certainty of a man who has already decided the matter. He offers the younger sister as consolation, as though a wife were an object to be swapped. But he has made a fatal mistake: he has chosen to harden Samson's wound rather than heal it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "This time I will be blameless"—there's a terrible logic here. Samson believes that if the Philistines strike first, his revenge is justified. We convince ourselves of such things when anger has begun to drive us. Yet justice in the hand of the wounded is never quite just.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three hundred foxes—a staggering feat of will and labor. Samson binds their tails together with torch-bearing precision. There's dark creativity in this violence. Yet pause and see: such elaborate schemes of revenge always require more foxes, more fire, more hands tied together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The fire spreads from grain to standing crops to olive groves—the livelihood of a people burns. Samson has moved from personal hurt to collective harm. How swiftly revenge scales itself when we step out of the light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Philistines burn his wife and her father in return. It is a cruelty that matches his own cruelty grain for grain. But now there are ashes where there was once a woman, and Samson has learned a terrible lesson: revenge multiplies, and the innocent pay the price.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will take revenge on you, and after that I will cease." Samson speaks as though there is a stopping point, as though one final act of vengeance will restore peace. But the cycle has no natural end—only the grace of God can break it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Etam's rock becomes his refuge—a cave where a man can hide from the consequences of his own strength. Yet the cave is also a prison. Samson has fled to safety, but what kind of life is lived in hiding, no matter how strong the man who hides?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lehi becomes a name forever linked with this conflict. When we act in anger, we mark places and people with our violence. The Philistines spread themselves across the land—and all because one man could not release his grip on what was taken from him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The men of Judah ask why the Philistines have come. They are about to discover that one man's vendetta can bring war to a nation. This is the hidden cost of unbroken strength: it draws conflict, and others must pay.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three thousand men of Judah descend to the cave. They do not come to comfort Samson but to bind him—their own brother—and hand him to the enemy. Such is the isolation that follows when a man's strength becomes his own nation's burden.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even at this moment, Samson asks for a promise: "Swear to me that you will not attack me yourselves." He cannot trust his own people. He demands their oath while he plans to go into captivity. There is a profound loneliness in being the strongest man in a room that fears you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two new ropes bind him—strong cordage, yet they hold him only because he permits it. His brothers swear they will not kill him, only deliver him. Even in compromise, there is a wound: they hand him over to those who would.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the Philistines shout, the Spirit of the Lord comes upon him, and the ropes fall like ash. It is a moment of divine visitation in the midst of human folly. Yet mark this carefully: God's strength flows through Samson, but Samson's choices remain his own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A fresh jawbone of a donkey—the humblest of weapons in the hand of the strongest of men. He takes it up and strikes a thousand. What a strange image: power magnified through whatever is at hand, indiscriminate in its force.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Samson sings of his victory: heaps upon heaps, a thousand men. Yet listen beneath the words—there is a peculiar hollowness to such boasting. A man who must sing of his own strength is confessing something he would rather hide.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ramath Lehi—"Jawbone Hill"—a name given to mark the place of slaughter. We name our victories, our battlefields, the spots where we prove ourselves. Yet do we ever return to such places in peace, or only to remember why we cannot rest?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Samson is thirsty—undone not by the enemy but by thirst. He cries to the Lord: "Have I done this only to fall now?" There is a desperation here, a sudden awareness that strength is not enough. He who has struck down a thousand is helpless before his own body's need.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God splits the hollow place in Lehi, and water flows. It is a small miracle, precise to the need of the moment. Yet see how even here mercy comes not as reward for righteousness but as sustenance for weakness. En Hakkore—the Caller's Spring—marks a place where God answers a man who finally cries out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twenty years Samson judged Israel. Readers today hear an echo in this—how often do we find ourselves preserved in our strength long after the moment we needed mercy? Samson is given a long life of power, yet the deepest victory might have been the one he never won.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
